Contact of Bulk Carrier Belle Mer Anchor with
Subsea Cable
On November 15, 2024, about 1211 local time, the cargo vessel Belle Mer was
anchored in the Tongass Narrows, near Ketchikan, Alaska, when the ship dragged
anchor and damaged a subsea fiber optic cable (see figure 1 and figure 2).1 There
were no injuries, and no pollution was reported. There was no damage to the vessel.
Damage to the subsea cable was estimated at $240,000.

1 Factual Information
1.1 Background
The 591-foot-long Belle Mer was a bulk carrier constructed of steel and built by
Tsuneishi Group Shipbuilding in Zhoushan, China, in 2021. The vessel was owned by
Reitaku Kaiun Co, Ltd and Belle Maritime S.A., and operated by Filteam
Shipmanagement, Inc.
The Tongass Narrows is a body of water located between Gravina Island and
Revillagigedo Island, Alaska, in the Clarence Strait. A subsea fiber optic cable, Alaska
United Southeast Cable Segment 2 (AUSE-2), connected the cities of Ketchikan and
Wrangell, Alaska, and lay along the bottom of the Tongass Narrows (see figure 2).2
The cable was owned and maintained by GCI Communication Corp.
1.2 Event Sequence
On November 14, the Belle Mer was transiting southeast, bound for an
anchorage site near Mud Bay in the Tongass Narrows, where it would onload a cargo
of timber. While the Belle Mer was at anchorage, the logs would be floated from a
nearby shoreside facility and pulled to the Belle Mer using assist boats.
About 0455, a Southeast Alaska Pilots’ Association (SEAPA) pilot and two pilot
observers (pilots in training) boarded the Belle Mer near the Guard Island Light in the
Clarence Strait, 12 statute miles northwest of Ketchikan.3 The master and pilot
conducted a master/pilot exchange, and the ship met an assist tug, which was then
positioned on the Belle Mer’s port bow to assist with anchoring.4

The area chosen for the Belle Mer to anchor in the Tongass Narrows was not a
common anchoring site. Most piloted traffic in the Tongass Narrows was cruise ships
transiting through the area to dock in and near downtown Ketchikan. There were no
US Coast Guard-designated anchorages near Mud Bay. The nearest designated
anchorage, Ketchikan Harbor Anchorage Area, was 6 miles to the southeast, making
it less desirable for the Belle Mer’s intended cargo operations.
The pilot, who had been a SEAPA pilot since 2007 and had experience
anchoring cruise ships in the Tongass Narrows, told investigators that this was the first
time he had anchored a vessel in this exact location. He recalled that smaller vessels,
such as yachts, and at least one other logging vessel had been anchored near the
Belle Mer’s location. The pilot stated that the stevedores and agents had requested
the final anchoring location. Although nautical charts for the area outlined a cable
area nearby where anchoring was restricted, he agreed to the requested location
because it balanced the safety of the vessel with the requests of the stevedores and
was outside of the anchoring-restricted area, all without impeding vessel traffic. The
master, who had joined the Belle Mer a month prior, had never sailed in Alaska
before and deferred to the pilot about the anchoring location.
While the pilot was conning the vessel to the anchoring location, the weather
was calm. Winds were recorded at 5–10 knots, changing from the northwest to the
southeast at Ketchikan International Airport (about 5 statute miles southeast of the
anchoring location). The current in the area was slack, rising to 1.2 knots of flood at
0902. The pilot told investigators that he had checked the weather forecasts, noting
increased winds expected for the next day. He shared this information with the
master and offered guidance on preparing the vessel for the change in weather,
telling him he could deploy 2 extra shots (about 180 feet) of anchor chain if needed.5
According to the pilot, this practice was “quite a normal procedure.”
As the ship neared the anchoring location, the pilot instructed the crew to walk
out 2 shots of anchor chain on deck and make the starboard anchor ready for letting
go.6 (The Belle Mer was fitted with two stockless anchors, one each on the port and
starboard sides of the bow.7 The starboard anchor was connected to 12 shots [about

1.3 Additional Information
1.3.1 Damage
The Belle Mer sustained no structural damage or damage to ground tackle
equipment during the casualty. Nineteen of the 24 fibers in the AUSE-2 subsea fiber
optic cable were damaged. GCI estimated repairs to the cable were $240,000.

2 Analysis
On November 15, 2024, while the bulk carrier Belle Mer was anchored in the
Tongass Narrows near Ketchikan, Alaska, the vessel began dragging anchor during a
3-hour period of sustained high winds, and about 1226, the vessel’s anchor contacted
AUSE-2, a subsea fiber optic cable.
2.1 Anchoring Location
On November 14, under the guidance of a SEAPA pilot, the Belle Mer
approached the requested anchoring area in the Tongass Narrows, from the
northeast. The pilot communicated with a stevedore in a nearby small boat, and the
two agreed on an acceptable anchoring location. The master, who was unfamiliar
with the Tongass Narrows, deferred to the pilot.
The ship was moved into position to begin anchoring. The Belle Mer’s engines
were ordered astern and the forward headway stopped about 0554. The order to let
go the starboard anchor was also given about this time. The AIS data and common
anchoring practice indicate that the location of the starboard hawsepipe about 0554
is the likely location where the anchor initially rested on the seafloor.
The pilot reported he felt the chosen location was suitable and estimated the
anchor was 300 feet from the border of a cable area (which marked the location of
AUSE-2). Cable areas on nautical charts mark zones where one or more
telecommunications or power cables are lying on, or buried in, the seafloor.
Anchoring is restricted or prohibited in cable areas to protect undersea cables from
damage by anchors. When the Belle Mer’s starboard anchor was let go, the bow of
the ship was about 190 feet east, and outside of, the charted cable area—about
110 feet closer to the cable area than the pilot had estimated. Based on AIS data and
“as laid” survey data, the NTSB estimates the location where the anchor was dropped
and initially rested was as close as 445 feet from AUSE-2.
In addition, the anchor’s location fell within a charted dumping ground (see
figure 5). Although anchoring in a dumping ground is not prohibited, it is inadvisable
due to the unpredictable depth and composition of the seafloor in such an area.
When agreeing to an anchoring location, the pilot and master should have
considered the distance to the charted hazard (subsea cable) and the suitability of the
seafloor for anchoring, accounting for possible drag.
Ten shots of chain were deployed while the Belle Mer moved astern. When the
Belle Mer’s astern momentum stopped about 0611, the pilot reported that the ship
took a “good, strong strain” on the chain.

2.2 Anchor Chain Scope
In addition to proximity to hazards and suitability of the seafloor, pilots and
masters should consider the water depth, the length of available anchor chain, and
forecasted weather conditions when they plan to anchor. Maintaining adequate
scope—the ratio of the length of anchor chain deployed from the ship to the depth of
the water under the bow of the vessel—ensures that an anchor’s designed holding
power is achieved and prevents dragging.12 Deploying a length of anchor chain with
a scope of 5:1 to 7:1 is recommended; even more anchor chain is recommended in
adverse weather.13
The ship anchored at a depth of 220 feet. The crew deployed 900 feet
(10 shots) of the available 1,080 feet (12 shots) of the starboard anchor chain; the
deployed chain’s scope was about 4:1. To anchor a vessel in moderate conditions, a
scope of 5:1 (1,100 feet; 12.2 shots) to 7:1 (1,540 feet, 17 shots) is recommended. If
the crew had deployed the remaining 2 shots, the chain’s scope would have been
closer (4.9:1) to the minimum but still under the lower end of the recommended
range. Additionally, given the forecasted adverse weather (increased wind speeds),
more scope would have been prudent. Therefore, given the water depth, the
starboard anchor chain’s scope was inadequate for both moderate conditions and
the high winds on the day of the casualty.
The day after the Belle Mer anchored, wind speeds and the tide were higher
than the previous day, and the vessel’s AIS positions relative to its anchor’s location
reflected a vessel whose anchor chain was under tension. Given the chain’s
inadequate scope, it is likely the anchor chain had minimal catenary. When a chain
has minimal catenary, the holding power of the anchoring system (chain and anchor)
is negatively affected. The chain’s frictional holding power is nearly eliminated (as the
chain is lifted from the seafloor) and the reduced angle at which the anchor chain
pulls on the anchor decreases the effective holding power of the anchor. Diminished
holding power, in turn, increases the likelihood of the anchor unseating and
dragging. Due to anchor chain scope, the Belle Mer likely dragged anchor into the
nearby restricted area until the anchor struck AUSE-2.

drag circle should be plotted using the location of the anchor drop. However, the
crew plotted the drag circle’s center 465 feet northwest of where the NTSB estimated
the anchor was dropped about 0554. Investigators noted that the plotted location
corresponded with the location of the ship’s GPS antenna at 0554. Therefore, it is
possible the crew incorrectly used the location of the GPS antenna rather than the
location where the anchor was dropped.

Investigators also noted that the radius of the crew’s plotted drag circle
matched the distance to the nearest shoal water—0.35 miles—from that plotted anchor
location. Shoal waters lined the coast near the anchoring location the stevedore
requested and were visible on the vessel’s ECDIS display, and the crew would have
known to avoid the areas (see figure 9). It is possible that the borders of the plotted
drag circle were based on proximity to shoal water. However, the master was unable
to explain the crew’s process for plotting drag circles, and no other crewmembers
were interviewed. Therefore, the exact method the Belle Mer crew used to plot the
vessel’s drag circle could not be determined.

On November 15, about 1211, the vessel was 1,395 feet from the actual
anchoring location. For the next 15 minutes, the vessel moved in a northwesterly
direction, past the cable. No ECDIS alarms alerted the crew during this time because
the vessel never exceeded the bounds of the drag circle they plotted. The crew’s drag
circle, which was not based on the length of anchor chain payed out or the distance
from the hawsepipe to the ship’s GPS antenna, was too large to effectively evaluate
whether the ship was dragging anchor. If the crew had correctly plotted the drag circle
radius, an ECDIS alarm may have notified the crew as the vessel moved past the circle’s
boundary. Without an audible alarm, the crew remained unaware that they were
dragging anchor. Had the crew properly plotted the drag circle correctly, they may
have had the opportunity to take action to attempt to avoid the anchor striking the
cable.

3 Conclusions
3.1 Probable Cause
The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause
of the anchor strike of bulk carrier Belle Mer with the Alaska United Southeast Cable
Segment 2 subsea fiber optic cable was the pilot and master’s choice to anchor near
a known restricted anchoring area with inadequate anchor chain scope given the
water depth and forecasted weather conditions. Contributing to the casualty was the
Belle Mer crew’s improperly plotted drag circle, which was too large and, therefore,
could not be used to effectively evaluate whether the ship was dragging anchor.
3.2 Lessons Learned
Anchoring Considerations
When choosing a suitable anchoring location, mariners must consider many
different criteria, including water depth, bottom type, proximity to hazards, weather,
and available anchor chain scope. Holding power of the anchor and anchor chain
also should be constantly analyzed while at anchor, especially under increasing
external forces (such as wind and current) and while anchored near charted hazards.
Additionally, drag and swing circles should be based on the actual anchor drop
location and accurate vessel and anchor chain measurements. Once accurate drag
and swing circles are plotted, mariners should continually monitor the vessel’s
position with regular fixes compared to the plotted drag circle, swing circle, and
available visual references.
